children: Rising fuel costs, strike-related expenses and mounting losses have prompted the German airline to intensify its restructuring efforts

German airline Lufthansa plans to eliminate 1,000 full-time positions at its flagship airline, Lufthansa Airlines, as mounting financial pressures and rising operating costs force the company to accelerate its restructuring efforts.

The proposed job cuts will affect operations at the airline's Frankfurt and Munich hubs and represent approximately 2.5 per cent of its workforce of around 40,000 employees. The announcement was communicated to employees through an internal letter signed by Lufthansa Airlines chief executive Jens Ritter and other senior executives.

The management attributed the decision to the airline's deteriorating financial position, citing persistently high fuel prices, strike-related expenses and an already elevated cost base. The company said its earlier turnaround measures were no longer sufficient to secure its long-term financial stability.
During the first nine months of 2026, Lufthansa Airlines recorded an operating loss of approximately €180 million, translating into average monthly losses of around €20 million.

The internal communication also highlighted the impact of the conflict in the Middle East, which has contributed to higher fuel costs, alongside nine days of strike action during the year. Management said these developments had further intensified the airline's operational and financial challenges.

The workforce reduction forms part of a broader efficiency drive that will also involve changes to the airline's flight operations and fleet strategy. Lufthansa plans to further reduce capacity on short and medium-haul routes and reduce the number of Airbus A320-family aircraft in its fleet, partially replacing them with smaller and more fuel-efficient Airbus A220 aircraft.
The airline is also accelerating the installation of Starlink satellite-based internet connectivity across its fleet, aiming to generate additional revenue through onboard connectivity services.

The latest announcement follows Lufthansa Group's September 2025 plan to eliminate approximately 4,000 administrative positions by 2030, primarily through digitalisation and the consolidation of administrative functions. However, it remains unclear whether the newly announced 1,000 job reductions at Lufthansa Airlines are included in that earlier target or represent additional cuts.

The restructuring comes amid wider challenges for the European aviation industry, particularly from volatile fuel prices, labour disputes and increasing pressure to improve operational efficiency. Lufthansa has also been engaged in negotiations with pilot unions over pay and working conditions, with disagreements continuing over proposed employment terms.

Interestingly, the financial performance of the wider Lufthansa Group has been relatively stronger than that of its flagship airline. The group reported a 30 per cent increase in net profit during the July-September quarter, supported by demand for premium long-haul travel. However, the core Lufthansa Airlines business continues to face profitability challenges.

At the end of 2025, Lufthansa Group employed 103,255 people worldwide, with approximately 64 per cent working across its passenger airlines. The latest restructuring highlights the distinction between the group's overall financial performance and the continuing pressure on its flagship carrier to improve productivity, control costs and restore profitability.
